questions.question: Eric writes problems at a constant rate of 6 problems per hour, and Elizabeth solves problems at a constant rate of 10 problems per hour. If Eric starts writing problems 2 hours before Elizabeth starts solving problems, how many problems will he have written when Elizabeth ﬁnishes solving all the problems he has written so far?
questions.solution: Answer: 30. Eric writes problems at a constant rate of 6 problems per hour, and Elizabeth solves problems at a constant rate of 10 problems per hour. If Eric starts writing problems 2 hours before Elizabeth starts solving problems, how many problems will he have written when Elizabeth ﬁnishes solving all the problems he has written so far? Answer: 30 Solution: After two hours, Eric will have written 12 problems. Letx be the number of hours that Elizabeth solves problems. Eric will have written 12+6 x problems, while Elizabeth will have solved 10x problems. This gives us the equation 12 + 6x = 10x, which solves to x = 3. Therefore, Elizabeth will have solved 10· 3 = 30 problems.

questions.question: Steve works 40 hours a week at his new job. He usually gets paid 8 dollars an hour, but if he works for more than 8 hours on a given day, he earns 12 dollars an hour for every additional hour over 8 hours. If x is the maximum number of dollars that Steve can earn in one week by working exactly 40 hours, and y is the minimum number of dollars that Steve can earn in one week by working exactly 40 hours, what is x − y?
questions.solution: Answer: 96. Steve works 40 hours a week at his new job. He usually gets paid 8 dollars an hour, but if he works for more than 8 hours on a given day, he earns 12 dollars an hour for every additional hour over 8 hours. If x is the maximum number of dollars that Steve can earn in one week by working exactly 40 hours, and y is the minimum number of dollars that Steve can earn in one week by working exactly 40 hours, what is x − y? Answer: 96 Solution: In the minimum case, Steve can work 8 hours a day for ﬁve days, thereby earning no overtime pay and earning exactly $320. In the maximum case, Steve works 40 hours without a single break. This spans two days; there are 16 hours of work at regular pay and 24 hours of work at overtime pay. Therefore, Steve earns 16 × $8 + 24 × $12 = $416. Therefore, x = 416 and y = 320, so x − y = 96 .

questions.question: Eric has a 9-sided dice and Harrison has an 11-sided dice. They each roll their respective die. Eric wins if he rolls a number greater or equal to Harrison’s number. What is the probability Eric wins?
questions.solution: Answer: 5. Eric has a 9-sided dice and Harrison has an 11-sided dice. They each roll their respective die. Eric wins if he rolls a number greater or equal to Harrison’s number. What is the probability Eric wins? Answer: 5 11 Solution: There are 9· 11 = 99 possible combinations of rolls. We then count the number of ways Eric can win: • If Eric rolls a 1, Harrison must roll a 1. • If Eric rolls a 2, Harrison must roll a 1 or 2. • In general, if Eric rolls an n, then Harrison must roll any number between 1 and n, for a total of n possible rolls. Thus, the number of combinations where Eric wins is 1 + 2 + ··· + 9 = 45. The probability Eric wins is therefore 45 99 = 5 11 .

questions.question: A number is formed using the digits {2, 0, 1, 8}, using all 4 digits exactly once. Note that 0218 = 218 is a valid number that can be formed. What is the probability that the resulting number is strictly greater than 2018?
questions.solution: Answer: 11. A number is formed using the digits {2, 0, 1, 8}, using all 4 digits exactly once. Note that 0218 = 218 is a valid number that can be formed. What is the probability that the resulting number is strictly greater than 2018? Answer: 11 24 Solution: There are 4! = 24 total possible permutations of the digits {2, 0, 1, 8}. Next, we count the number of cases where the permutation is greater than 2018. When the leftmost digit is an 8, the permutation must be greater than 2018, and there are 3! = 6 such per- mutations. When the leftmost digit is a 2, the permutation is not greater than 2018 only when the permutation is 2018 itself, since 0 < 1< 8. In this case, there are 3! − 1 = 5 such permutations. Because all other permutations of the digits have a thousands digit which is less than 2, the desired probability is 6+5 24 = 11 24 .

questions.question: Ted has 2 red socks, 2 blue socks, and 2 green socks. He grabs three diﬀerent socks at random. Compute the probability that they are all diﬀerent colors.
questions.solution: Answer: 2. Ted has 2 red socks, 2 blue socks, and 2 green socks. He grabs three diﬀerent socks at random. Compute the probability that they are all diﬀerent colors. Answer: 2 5 Solution: Ted ﬁrst draws one sock. With probability 4 5, the second sock he draws will not match the ﬁrst sock. With probability 2 4, the third sock he draws matches neither the ﬁrst sock nor the second sock. Therefore, with probability 4 5· 2 4 = 2 5 , the three socks will all be diﬀerent colors.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 2019 2019 is divided by 7?
questions.solution: Answer: 6. What is the remainder when 2019 2019 is divided by 7? Answer: 6 Solution: Note that 2019≡ 3 mod 7. So, we have 2019 2019≡ 32019 mod 7. Then Fermat’s Little Theorem gives us that 3 a≡ 3b mod 7 if a≡ b mod 6. So, we ﬁnd that 2019 ≡ 3 mod 6. Thus, 2019 2019≡ 27≡ 6 mod 7.

questions.question: You need to bike to class but don’t know where you parked your bike. There are two bike racks, A and B. There is a 1 /5 chance for your bike to be at A; it takes one minute to walk to A and four minutes to bike from A to class. Then, there is a 4 /5 chance for your bike to be at B; it takes three minutes to walk to B and five minutes to bike from B to class. However, if your choice is wrong, you need to walk from your original choice A or B to the other, which takes four minutes, before departing to class from there. SMT 2022 General Test April 16–17, 2022 Suppose you only care about getting to class on time. For a some interval of minutes before class, going to bike rack B first gives a strictly higher chance of making it to class on time. How many minutes long is that interval (i.e. an interval of 15 minutes before class to 21 minutes before class has length 6)?
questions.solution: Answer: 2. You need to bike to class but don’t know where you parked your bike. There are two bike racks, A and B. There is a 1 /5 chance for your bike to be at A; it takes one minute to walk to A and four minutes to bike from A to class. Then, there is a 4 /5 chance for your bike to be at B; it takes three minutes to walk to B and five minutes to bike from B to class. However, if your choice is wrong, you need to walk from your original choice A or B to the other, which takes four minutes, before departing to class from there. Suppose you only care about getting to class on time. For a some interval of minutes before class, going to bike rack B first gives a strictly higher chance of making it to class on time. How many minutes long is that interval (i.e. an interval of 15 minutes before class to 21 minutes before class has length 6)? Answer: 2 Solution: If you go to bike rack A first, then there is a 1/5 chance that your bike is there and you get to class in 1 + 4 = 5 minutes. Otherwise, there is a 4 /5 chance that your bike is not there, and you get to class in 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 minutes. If you go to bike rack B first, then there is a 4 /5 chance that your bike is there and you get to class in 3 + 5 = 8 minutes. Otherwise, there is a 1/5 chance that your bike is not there, and you get to class in 3 + 4 + 4 = 11 minutes. If there are less than 5 minutes before class, then both options give you no chance of getting to class on time. If there are between 5 and 8 minutes before class, then going to bike rack A gives you a 1/5 chance of making it to class on time, while going to bike rack B gives you no chance of making it to class on time. If there are between 8 and 10 minutes before class, then going to bike rack A still gives you a 1/5 chance of making it to class on time, while going to bike rack B now gives you a 4/5 chance of making it to class on time. If there are more than 10 minutes before class starts, then going to bike rack A will always lead to you making it to class on time, which means going to bike rack B will never give you a strictly greater chance of making it to class on time. Thus, going to bike rack B is better only if there are between 8 and 10 minutes before class, which is an interval of 2 minutes.

Ice cream protrudes from the top of the cone in a perfect hemisphere. Find the surface area of the ice cream cone, ice cream included, in square inches. SMT 2013 General Test February 2, 2013
questions.solution: Answer: 5π. Sara has an ice cream cone with every meal. The cone has a height of 2 √ 2 inches and the base of the cone has a diameter of 2 inches. Ice cream protrudes from the top of the cone in a perfect hemisphere. Find the surface area of the ice cream cone, ice cream included, in square inches. Answer: 5π SMT 2013 General Test Solutions February 2, 2013 Solution: The radius of the cone is 2 2 = 1, so the lateral height of the cone is √ 12 + (2 √ 2)2 = 3 and the lateral surface area of the cone is π· 1· 3 = 3π. Next, the surface area of the hemisphere is 2πr2 = 2π. Thus, the total surface area is 2 π + 3π = 5π .

questions.solution: Answer: 30. Imagine that school starts at 8:00 AM. When you drive at 50 mph, you reach 12 minutes early, but when you drive at 40 mph, you reach at 8:15. How many miles do you live from school? Answer: 30 Solution: We can set up a system of equations where t represents how long it would take you to reach school if you planned to reach exactly at 8 : 00 AM. Since distance = rate * time, we can let d equal the total distance from home to school. Then we have d = 50∗ (t− 1 5) and d = 40∗ (t + 1 4). Solving this, we get that t = 2 and d = 90.

questions.question: Let a 5 digit number be termed a “valley” number if the digits (not necessarily distinct) in the number a b c d e satisfy a > b > c and c < d < e . Compute the number of valley numbers that start with 3. SMT 2014 General Test February 15, 2014

Compute the number of valley numbers that start with 3. Answer: 100 Solution: b, c can be 2 , 1, 2, 0, or 1 , 0. If c = 1, 2≤ d≤ 9 and d + 1≤ e≤ 9 and hence there are 7 + 6 +... + 1 = 28 possibilities (alternately, this is equivalent to choosing two distinct digits in the range 2 through 9 for a total of (8 2 ) = 28 possibilities). Similarly, for c = 0 there are 8 + 7 + ... + 1 = 36 possibilities (or (9 2 ) = 36 possibilities). Since there are two ways to obtain c = 0 and one way to obtain c = 1, there are 28 + 36 + 36 = 100 valley numbers.

questions.question: An icosahedron is a regular polyhedron with 12 vertices, 20 faces, and 30 edges. How many rigid rotations G are there for an icosahedron in R3?
questions.solution: Answer: 60. An icosahedron is a regular polyhedron with 12 vertices, 20 faces, and 30 edges. How many rigid rotations G are there for an icosahedron in R3? Answer: 60 There are 12 vertices, each with 5 neighbors. Any vertex and any of its neighbors can be rotated to any other vertex-neighbor pair in exactly one way. There are 5 · 12 = 60 vertex-neighbor pairs.

questions.question: Consider the sequence of integers {an}n≥1 constructed in the following way. a1≥ 1, and for n≥ 2 we have an = (a2 n−1 + 337an−1) modulo 2022. We define the period of a sequence to be the smallest integer k such that there is an integer N such that for all n≥ N we have an+k = an. Determine the sum of all possible periods of an.
questions.solution: Answer: 12. Consider the sequence of integers {an}n≥1 constructed in the following way. a1≥ 1, and for n≥ 2 we have an = (a2 n−1 + 337an−1) modulo 2022. We define the period of a sequence to be the smallest integerk such that there is an integerN such that for alln≥N we havean+k =an. Determine the sum of all possible periods of an. Answer: 12 Solution: We will break our problem down using the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Taking our expression in mod 2 and 3, we find that our recursion is an≡a2 n−1 +an−1 (mod 2, 3), which is easily seen to have a period 1 in both residues. Therefore, our period depends only on the sequence in mod 337. Taking our expression mod 337 we have thatan≡a2 n−1 (mod 337). Let k be the period of an. Then there is sufficiently large d such thatad≡ad+k (mod 337). In other words ad≡a2k d =⇒ ord337(ad)|2k−1 (mod 337). But we also have that ord(ad)|ϕ(337) = 336 = 2 4∗ 3∗ 7, which implies that ord( ad)∈{ 1, 3, 7, 21}. Taking the minimumk that satisfy these conditions we have that we can have k = 1, 2, 3, 6. We need only show that these are all possible periods. Clearly a period of length 1 is possible since we could have a1 = 1. To obtain a period of length 2 we note that takinga1 = 128 gives the sequence 128, 208, 128,... . To obtain a period of length 3, observe that taking a1 = 8 gives the sequence 8, 64, 52, 8,... . To obtain a period of length 6, note that taking a1 = 2 gives the sequence 2, 4, 16, 256, 158, 26, 2,... . Hence our answer is 12 . SMT 2022 General Test Solutions April 16–17, 2022
